trajectory_summary: This is a short, transactional recovery call: the customer called back annoyed about repeated contact, and the rep converted that irritation into a booked appointment in under two minutes. Energy moved from complaint to compliant booking, but almost entirely through logistics — no interest question, no bill, no prior-design probe, no button-up completion. It's a fast save, not a strong set.

observed_outcome.quote: Maybe ten. I should be free.
observed_outcome.reasoning: A specific day (Monday) and time (10AM) were stated and both sides agreed, but the customer's own phrasing ('Maybe ten. I should be free') signals soft, unconfirmed commitment, and button-up was left incomplete (no is-that-fair handshake, no full recap) — consistent with a fragile/tentative set despite a nominal time being captured.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: No bill amount or usage was asked for or provided on the call, so no flip was possible.

bill_document_audit.reasoning: The rep did not request the customer's utility bill or instructions for sending it.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep did not ask why the customer was interested in solar; the customer did not volunteer a motivating reason.

objections.quote: You've called me six times. I'm wondering what if there's something wrong.
attempt_quotes: Okay. Yeah. It looks like, it looks like we were reaching out because we had put together a solar design for your home.

objections.reasoning: Customer's repeated-calls complaint stalled the script until the rep offered a scheduling fix and, finally, a direct apology; customer accepted and booked, so it resolved but late.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: Skipped the interest/bill re-anchor entirely on a warm re-engagement call
primary_coaching_focus.quote: it looks like we were reaching out because we had put together a solar design for your home.
primary_coaching_focus.why: This is a customer with an existing design already calling back — a high-value anchor — yet the rep never asks about current interest, bill pain, or what happened with the prior design; the whole call runs on scheduling logistics alone, leaving the appointment thin and easy to no-show.

key_moments.stewart_read: This is the excessive_contact_complaint protocol — a real operational friction, not a sales objection — and the rep should resolve it early via action, not defense.

key_moments.quote: And now I've had five more people call me.
key_moments.stewart_read: Second touch on the same contact-frequency complaint; rep offers a scheduling fix but still doesn't apologize or explain why the promised callback never happened.

key_moments.quote: sorry for all the phone calls. I know our dialer is kind of aggressive
key_moments.stewart_read: Third touch: the apology finally lands, but only after the appointment is locked — sequencing suggests it was a closing courtesy, not genuine resolution.

key_moments.quote: Well, last year. It depends what address, I guess.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer signals ambiguity/multiple properties or uncertainty about the prior design; rep confirms the address but never asks what the customer thought of the design or whether they're still interested in it.
